For this reason, he rejects the colonial claim that Africa has no history of civilization. He writes:

“In this field of research, which is so valuable for the study of thought itself, we are now beginning to discover that most of Africa was not savage, as people once believed. Even while isolated in desert or forest, it exerted influence in different directions, and influences travelled from the Nile through Libya, Nubia, and Ethiopia.”

Throughout the book, we also find a sound understanding of the objective relationship between myth, religion, and philosophy—different forms of social consciousness—and the reality of humanity’s material activity.
Masson-Oursel also firmly rejects the “theory” that divides human beings into separate racial groups, arguing that “pure groups exist only in a few narrowly defined cases.”
Richard Walzer followed a similar method in an extensive study of Islamic philosophy.

He carefully identified both its external sources and its internal ones. He rejected two equally unhistorical positions: the claim that Islamic philosophy was a purely Arab creation, and the opposite claim that it was produced solely from Greek philosophical sources.

“The time has not yet come to write a definitive history of Islamic philosophy. Our knowledge of this philosophy has not yet reached the maturity and completeness needed for such a vast undertaking. Many facts remain unknown, and many works have been neglected for centuries...”

He was also right to say that understanding the character of the main cultural sources of Islamic philosophy “is essential if we are to understand the original and individual solutions that Arab philosophers gave to the philosophical problems they addressed.”
His mistake, however, was that he concentrated mainly on the external sources. He mentioned the internal sources only briefly and indirectly.

For example, he writes that “al-Fārābī’s interest in Plato arose from specifically Islamic problems that existed in his own time, and this interest helped him reach an original and influential solution.”

He also says that when Islamic philosophers absorbed Greek thought in a productive way, “their work was a serious attempt to transform this foreign body of thought, so different from the Islamic heritage, and make it a living part of Islamic culture.”
But the actual nature of those problems, and of this “Islamic heritage,” remains unclear.
Another sound feature of Walzer’s method appears when he says:

“The more we learn about human history, the more we realize that nothing in history creates itself from nothing. History gives new forms to materials that already existed. Islamic philosophy is one workshop in this process through which human civilization continues.”
It is important to add, however, that Walzer’s study as a whole still begins from idealist and bourgeois positions. Because of this, it contains a number of weaknesses in method.

For example, he was right to reject the idea that foreign works were translated simply because the caliphs had a personal “thirst for knowledge.” But he failed to identify what we regard as the real cause: the needs of social development itself required scientific knowledge to develop. Instead, Walzer merely says that the cause “is not clear.”
He also explains the differences between the “Arab philosophers”—whether a particular thinker leaned more toward Neoplatonism or toward Aristotelianism—as a matter of “personal temperament.”
In doing so, he fails to take account of the wider conditions that made those differences necessary.

Maurice De Wulf, despite his own commitment to neo-Thomism, took a positive view of Arab-Islamic philosophy on several points. He rejected the claim that it was simply a copy of Peripatetic philosophy, arguing that Arab philosophers developed an independent approach to the problem of existence. Nor did he overlook the implication of the theory of emanation in the philosophy of al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā: that matter is eternal, rather than something newly created through emanation from the highest intellect. De Wulf also recognized that al-Ghazālī rejected rational knowledge in favour of theology bound by religious doctrine. Yet al-Ghazālī still remained committed to philosophical ways of thinking, even as he made them serve the doctrines of faith.

The great Orientalist Hamilton A. Gibb was burdened by metaphysical prejudices about Western thought and the Arab mind. Even so, he sometimes approached Islamic history in more realistic terms. He observed, for example, that Islam took different forms in different times and places under the influence of local geographical, social and political conditions. He was right to apply this idea when examining the distinctive features of the different regions where Islam existed as a social order, a culture and a religion.

When discussing Sufism, Gibb also tried to trace its links with ordinary people, especially rural communities and urban craftsmen. He was unable to see the class roots of this relationship, and so he could not recognize the revolutionary side of the Islamic Sufi movement. But his explanation at least pointed in that direction from a distance. He described Sufism as an attempt “to preserve the ideal unity of all Muslims.”

When he discussed the development of subversive Sufi tendencies within organized Sufism, and their continuation in two philosophical forms—Illuminationism in al-Suhrawardī and a philosophy of unity in Ibn ʿArabī—he wrote:

“The consequences of these two philosophies were extremely serious. Instead of renewing the substance of teaching in the schools, the Sufis redirected intellectual energies toward inward contemplation opposed to rational inquiry, without replacing it with a rigorous system...”
These historical observations deserve attention even though we disagree with the intellectual and methodological assumptions behind them.

When we turn to the more positive current within Orientalist scholarship and its attitude toward our philosophical heritage, the French scholar A. M. Goichon stands out. She was not only a scholar of philosophy in the Orientalist tradition, but also a highly capable philosophical researcher with a strong command of her subject. She read Arab-Islamic philosophical texts with great care and had an especially precise understanding of their terminology.
She also avoided the position shared by the three earlier trends, all of which were in harmony with the ideological outlook of imperialism.

These strengths appear clearly in her valuable lectures on Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy and in one of her studies of Ibn Sīnā’s Definitions. We can acknowledge these qualities in Goichon’s work without reservation.

In her lecture on “The Great Themes of Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy,” she rejects a claim that became widespread among Orientalists and was later repeated by most modern Arab researchers. According to this claim, the Ibn Sīnā of Remarks and Admonitions contradicts the Ibn Sīnā of The Healing. He supposedly began as a Peripatetic philosopher in The Healing, then ended his career as a mystical Illuminationist in Remarks and Admonitions and in his symbolic stories: The Treatise of the Bird, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Salāmān and Absāl, and the Treatise on Love.
The purpose of this claim is to bring Ibn Sīnā’s idealist side to the foreground while obscuring his materialist side.

Goichon rejects the idea that Ibn Sīnā contains this kind of contradiction. She argues that Remarks and Admonitions, although written late in his life and very different in appearance from The Healing, does not contradict the main lines of thought found in that earlier work.

She also points out that although Ibn Sīnā says in the introduction to The Logic of the Easterners that The Healing was no longer sufficient to express his own thought, he also says in that same work that The Healing contains everything the general body of philosophers needs.
Goichon takes this to mean that Ibn Sīnā remained committed to a rationalist line of thought in The Logic of the Easterners, just as he had been in The Healing.

She supports this by pointing out that the surviving pages of this incomplete work, only recently discovered, clearly follow the same general intellectual direction as Ibn Sīnā’s other writings. She goes further and argues that his shorter treatises, occasional writings and smaller works, taken together, provide important evidence for the same conclusion.

She also rejects the claim that Ibn Sīnā deliberately chose an “esoteric mode of presentation.” In her view, the differences among his works are more limited. Some are written as works of philosophy in the strict sense. In others, Ibn Sīnā allows his thought to move beyond the normal boundaries of philosophy in a mystical direction—but one so strongly rational in form that it would still be wrong to call him a mystic. It is possible, she suggests, that Ibn Sīnā did not wish to explain his position openly, or that he never had the freedom to write a precise work devoted to it.
Goichon keeps the same position in her detailed treatment of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy of existence.

Even when she discusses his theory of the soul, she does not regard his belief that the soul is a separate substance which survives the death of the body and lives a life close to that of the pure intellects as evidence of mysticism. Her reason is that Ibn Sīnā bases the soul’s eternal happiness on knowledge. The soul earns that happiness through the proper use of reason in the material world.

So, in her words, “the idea of happiness in heaven, and of misery in hell where intellects are deprived of knowledge of intelligible things, is entirely rational. In that case, it is impossible to identify a specifically Avicennian mysticism or determine its nature in the way people often claim.”
Goichon finally concludes that, for Ibn Sīnā, there is no reality apart from existence. Essences that have not yet received existence have no reality in themselves.

After following Ibn Sīnā’s texts closely on the question of existence and essence, she concludes that his philosophy is internally consistent. “Ibn Sīnā’s great mind,” she writes, “placed itself at a point from which his work appears as a single coherent whole,” and that work is “very far from being merely a translation of Aristotelian theories into Arabic.”
Finally, it is fair to say that supporters of this positive trend are not a rare exception among Orientalists. But it would be difficult to review all of their positions here.

Marxist Orientalists occupy a distinct place in the history of Orientalist scholarship because they approached our intellectual heritage in its different forms from an explicitly Marxist point of view. Their method was based on historical materialism, and their ideological outlook on scientific socialism.

For that reason, we do not find in their studies the same fundamental weaknesses that we found among other Western Orientalists and researchers, or among modern Arab researchers whose methods are idealist and ahistorical and whose ideological positions are imperialist or bourgeois.
This does not mean that Marxist studies contain no weaknesses at all.
As Marxists—or precisely because we are Marxists—we are, or should be, very far from making such an absolute claim.

Marxist researchers possess a method and an ideology that help them avoid the fundamental errors we have already discussed and illustrated. But the issue is not simply one of possessing the correct method as a theory or the correct ideology as a set of ideas. What matters after that is how the method is applied in practice.

Marxists proceed from a scientific conviction that historical materialism is valid, and that it is the only method capable of giving us scientific knowledge of our intellectual heritage. They also believe that such scientific knowledge alone is consistent with the ideology of the revolutionary proletariat, and that it can arm the mass base of the Arab liberation movement with an informed and constantly renewed political awareness. This is especially important in confronting the ideological struggle, which is becoming one of the central battlegrounds of our age.
They believe all this. But the real question remains the question of application.
This is where the individual researcher enters the picture.
Personal abilities are put to the test. The result may be success to varying degrees, or it may be failure.

The measure of success or failure is the distance between theory and application, between the method itself and the creative use of that method. The smaller this distance becomes, the greater the success. When the distance grows, failure begins.

This is where weaknesses appear in Marxist studies of the heritage. But compared with the fundamental weaknesses discussed earlier, these remain secondary. They do not arise from the method or ideology themselves. They come instead from a mechanical understanding of the method, from an incomplete view of the relationship between theory and concrete reality, or sometimes from a mismatch between a person’s intellectual commitments and their social position.
These secondary weaknesses may also arise for other reasons.

They may come from individual judgments about how general laws should be applied to a particular case. Such judgments may suffer from a lack of historical evidence about the specific case being studied. Or the case itself may be surrounded by distortions produced by outside forces.

This is exactly what has happened with the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage. Misleading studies separated this heritage from its indirect material and social foundations, leaving those foundations in the dark. As a result, modern generations—and even scientific researchers—have found it difficult to see the connection between the two.
Let us now move from the general point to a specific example.

A few pages ago we referred to the Marxist thesis that human society has developed, and continues to develop, through a series of historical stages. Each stage is defined by a particular form of social relations connected with material production. These forms follow, overlap with and grow out of one another along an upward but uneven historical path.
This view rests on the idea that relations of material production are the decisive factor shaping the movement of history.

When Marxism formulated this thesis, it drew on historical experience and on what it regarded as an objective agreement between that experience and the general laws of dialectical and historical materialism.
With the help of these laws, historical experience seemed to reveal a general pattern in human development. In broad terms, the sequence was:
primitive communism, then slave relations, then feudal relations, then capitalism, followed by socialism and finally the higher stage of scientific communism.
But does Marxism regard this pattern as a final and absolute truth?

Does it impose this sequence rigidly on every human society, as though the different social formations were ready-made moulds that every society must pass through in exactly the same way? Does it treat them as unavoidable stages that cannot vary, be skipped, overlap with other forms, or take on forms that are similar, different or even contrary to the familiar model?
We have already answered both questions.
First, we said that Marxism is not a rigid doctrine but a guide to action.

Second, when discussing this same theory of social formations, we said that the theory itself remains open to development whenever scientific research uncovers new features in historical experiences whose real character has not yet been fully understood.

Marxism says that absolute objective truth exists, but it also says that our knowledge of it is relative. In other words, our knowledge develops in stages. We gain it piece by piece as human awareness and science develop.
In this sense, absolute truth is made up of the accumulated results of relative truths, as Lenin put it.

So even in Marxist scientific thought itself, the familiar Marxist account of the social formations through which human society has developed is not a final formula expressing absolute objective truth in its entirety.
It still belongs to the realm of relative truths. It reflects the parts of historical reality that have become known so far. Other parts remain unknown.
We are not saying this as a digression. We are saying it because it leads directly to an example of the weaknesses that can appear in Marxist studies of medieval Arab-Islamic thought.
A Marxist researcher looking for the material foundations of this heritage may sometimes apply the familiar Marxist model of historical social formations too literally or mechanically.

The researcher may even invent a particular mode of production for which there is no historical basis, or whose features are unclear, or which had not yet fully developed, or which was actually a complex mixture of elements belonging to several different modes of production.

A mistake of this kind may come from an excessive desire to apply the Marxist model at any cost, even when the result is a “dogmatic” application that is foreign to Marxism’s own understanding of historical development.
One of the areas where Marxist researchers are most likely to fall into error or confusion is the answer to this question:

Which of the historical forms of social relations identified in the Marxist model best describes the social and economic relations of the Arabian Peninsula shortly before the rise of Islam, during the final period of the Jāhiliyya?
A similar problem appears when we ask about the true historical form of the mode of production under the Arab-Islamic state during the Umayyad and Abbasid periods.
Was it feudalism in the same form known in medieval Europe?
Was it a different form of feudalism?
Was it a distinctive mixture of slave, feudal and commercial relations?
Or was it something else entirely, with no direct equivalent among the traditional social formations familiar to Marxists?
Modern Marxist researchers—Arab scholars and Orientalists alike—often disagree on these questions.

That is because these are relatively new problems in Marxist studies of medieval Arab-Islamic society and of its intellectual movements. They are newer still in Marxist studies of Arab-Islamic philosophy, because Marxist work in this field began even later.

The very existence of these disagreements provides practical evidence that Marxist researchers do not treat the theory of social and economic formations as a final and absolute truth that can be applied in every detail, in exactly the same form, to every concrete situation in every historical period.
Nor do they treat it as a rigid ready-made formula to which every form of production and every kind of social relation in history must be mechanically forced to conform.

In fact, even the founders of Marxism, Marx and Engels, considered the possibility that other historical experiences—some only partly known in their own time, and others perhaps still to be discovered—might require changes in the way this theory was formulated.
Marx himself described one such historical form of property, which he said history showed us clearly. He called it “communal property” and described it as an “original form.”

Marx argued that property is “a condition of production,” and that “there can be no production, and therefore no society, without some form of property.” At the same time, however, he ridiculed the idea that this objective fact meant we had to “leap directly to one particular form of property, such as private property.”
